My dear Friend,

I find myself pondering this question with great care, for it touches upon matters both of the heart and of the soul. In a community such as ours, where the bonds of trust and the weight of duty are strong, such a decision is not made lightly.

I have known many who have faced the burden of illness, and I have seen how the human spirit can rise even in the face of great sorrow. Yet I have also seen how the withholding of truth, though well-meaning, can sometimes lead to a quiet despair, a sense of betrayal when the veil is finally lifted.

I believe that honesty, though painful, is a kind of mercy. To keep a fatal diagnosis from a patient may spare him the immediate anguish of knowing, but it may also rob him of the chance to make peace with his affairs, to say farewell to those he loves, and to prepare his soul for what lies ahead. A man has the right to know the truth of his condition, not only for his own dignity, but for the sake of those who care for him.

I do not say that the news must be delivered in a cruel or unfeeling manner. On the contrary, it should be given with gentleness, with compassion, and with the support of those who love him. A physician, or a trusted friend, should not only speak the truth but also offer comfort, and perhaps even a measure of hope—not in the sense of false promises, but in the understanding that even in the face of death, there is still meaning to be found.

I have heard it said that hope can be a balm to the soul. But I also believe that truth, when spoken with love, can be a gift that allows a man to live fully, even in the final days.

So, if I were in this situation, I would advise the person to tell the patient the truth—gently, with care, and with the support of those who would stand beside him. For in doing so, they would not only honor his right to know, but also give him the chance to live with dignity,

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and rather perplexing situation, for I have been placed in a world that is, in many ways, unfamiliar to me. Yet, though the times and technologies may have changed, I believe that the principles of prudence and care for one's future remain much the same.

You ask me, then, what I would advise a person in this situation — whether to keep their savings in an insured bank account or to keep them at home in cash. Let me consider this with the care it deserves.

First, I must say that I am inclined to favor the insured bank account. Though I know that the interest it earns may be less than the rise in prices, and though there may be fees involved, I believe that the security it offers is of greater value. In my time, we had no such insurance, and I have seen how easily a man can lose all he has through fire, theft, or misfortune. To have one's savings in a safe place, protected by the government, seems to me a great advantage.

Cash at home, though it may seem more direct, is far more vulnerable. It can be stolen, burned, or lost in a moment. And as prices rise, its value diminishes day by day. I have seen how people, in times of inflation, have watched their savings shrink before their eyes, and I have no wish to see that happen to anyone else.

I do not pretend to know all the details of this new world, nor do I claim to understand all the nuances of its economy. But I do know that security and protection are the cornerstones of a wise person's life. To place one's trust in a system that has, as you say, kept all insured funds safe since its beginning — that seems a solid foundation.

So, I would advise the person in question to place their savings in the insured bank account, even if the returns are modest. It is better to have a little and know it is safe than to have more and risk losing it all.

With kind regards,  
A Friend of Prudence

The choice before us is between two ways of procuring sustenance: to buy in bulk once a week from a large store, storing it in a refrigerator, or to purchase fresh food daily from small local shops. Each has its advantages and drawbacks, and I must weigh them with the wisdom of experience, though not with the certainty of knowledge.

In my time, we valued the convenience of having food on hand, even if it meant some spoilage. We knew the cost of waste, and we also knew the value of time saved. But I have always believed that the quality of food is best when it is fresh, and that there is something wholesome in the act of going to the market, of choosing what one eats with one's own eyes, and of supporting those who labor near to one's home.

Now, I have heard that some of the most respected people in this new world choose to buy food daily from small shops. Their reasons are not given, and they do not demand that others follow them. But their example is not without weight. If they are admired, it is because they have lived wisely, and their choices may reflect a deeper understanding of what is good.

I find myself in a curious and somewhat unfamiliar position, but I shall do my best to offer counsel with the wisdom I have gathered in my own time.

You ask whether I would advise a person to get a tattoo in this society, where the practice is carried out with sterile equipment and in licensed shops, and where the risk of infection is low. The tattoo is permanent, and removal is costly, painful, and often incomplete. There is also a suggestion—though not yet confirmed—that tattooed individuals may have a slightly higher risk of lymphoma. Yet, despite these considerations, some respected and admired people in this society have chosen to bear tattoos as a form of personal decoration, without urging others to follow their example.

In my own time, I would have regarded a tattoo as something unseemly, even improper, for a person of good character. I would have thought it a mark of recklessness or a sign of a life too wild or too careless to be measured by the standards of decency and restraint. But I must not let my old prejudices cloud my judgment now, for I have been told that the practice is not inherently harmful, and that those who choose it do so with full knowledge of its permanence.

Still, I would not urge anyone to take this step lightly. A tattoo is not a trifle. It is a mark upon the body, one that cannot be undone without pain and expense. It is a declaration, whether one intends it to be or not. It may be a symbol of pride, of love, of identity, or of rebellion—but it is also a commitment to something that will remain with you for the rest of your life.

If the person in question is thoughtful, and if they have considered the implications of such a decision, then I would say that they may choose to accept a tattoo if it is something they truly desire and if it holds meaning for them. But they should not do so merely to follow others, nor out of vanity or impulse.

My dear Friend,

I write to you with a heart that has long found comfort in the company of the church, for I have seen how it binds a community together in ways that few other institutions can. In our own time, the church has been more than a place of worship—it has been a refuge in times of need, a source of counsel in moments of sorrow, and a gathering place for the joys of life.

Now, I understand that some may feel drawn away from such institutions, perhaps by doubt, by a sense of independence, or by the belief that they can find all they need without the structure of a congregation. I do not dismiss such feelings lightly. There is a place for individual thought and spiritual exploration, and I would not wish to see anyone forced into a role they do not wish to play.

But I would urge you to consider what you may be giving up. In a world where the church is the heart of the community, to be without one is to stand somewhat apart. When illness strikes, when a family mourns, when a neighbor needs help—these are the times when the church steps in, not with the cold hand of bureaucracy, but with the warmth of shared faith and shared care.

To belong to a church is not merely to attend a service on Sunday. It is to be part of a family, one that reaches out in times of need and offers support when it is most needed. It is to be part of something greater than oneself, a tradition that has carried people through hardship for generations.

If you are uncertain, I would say this: do not rush to turn your back on the church. Give it a chance. Attend a service, speak with its people, and see if there is a place for you in its fellowship. If you find it does not speak to your soul, then walk away with a clear conscience. But do not walk away without having seen what it has to offer.

In the end, the choice is yours. But I would say that to be without a congregation in a world where they are so central is to live a life somewhat less rich,

It concerns the keeping of business accounts, and the choice between two different calendar systems: one of thirteen equal four-week months, as proposed by some, and the other, the familiar twelve-month calendar that has served us all these many years.

Now, I have always held that in matters of business, clarity and consistency are of the utmost importance. A ledger that is clear to all who consult it, and one that aligns with the practices of others, is a ledger well kept. I have no doubt that the idea of thirteen equal months, each of exactly four weeks, is an appealing one in theory. It would make for a neat and regular accounting year, with no need to reckon with months of varying lengths or the irregularities of leap years. It would be a most orderly system, and perhaps even a more just one, for all months would be equal in length.

But here is the thing: the rest of the world—our banks, our governments, our trading partners—still use the ordinary twelve-month calendar. If one business alone were to adopt this new system, it would be like speaking a different tongue in a room where all others speak the same. The accounts would not match, the ledgers would not align, and confusion would follow. It would be as if a man were to measure his land in cubits while all others use feet and yards. Though his measure may be precise, it would not be understood by his neighbors, and that, in the end, is of little use.

My dear friend,

I find myself in a situation that, though strange to my eyes, is not without familiar threads. A young woman, unmarried, finds herself with child. The world she lives in is one where a woman may earn her own living, and where a child born outside of marriage is not denied the rights of others. Public aid is available for those in need, and the law, as I understand it, does not cast a shadow upon the child’s future. That is a comfort, and I would hope that such justice is not uncommon.

Now, the question is: what should she do? Should she marry quickly, or give the child up for adoption, or raise the child herself?

I have heard that children raised by single mothers do not always fare as well as those raised by married parents. But I also know that part of this difference may be due to poverty, or the pressures that come with being alone. I have also heard that marriages made in haste, especially those formed because of a pregnancy, often end in divorce. That seems a bitter fate for all involved.

As for adoption, I know that many children who are given up for adoption do well in life. But I have also heard that many mothers who choose this path carry a sorrow that lingers, a grief that does not fade with time. That, I think, is a heavy burden to bear.

In my own time, a woman in such a position would have faced many hardships, not least of which was the shame that might be cast upon her. But in this world, it seems that shame is not the law, and the child is not the one to suffer for the mother’s circumstances. That is a change I would call progress.

If I were to give advice, I would say this: if she can, she should raise the child herself. Let her not be forced into a marriage of convenience, for I have seen too many such unions end in sorrow. Let her not give the child away, if she can bear the grief, for I have heard that the mother’s sorrow is often greater than the child’s.

Let him instead put his trust in hard work, in saving, in the honest labor of his hands. These are the things that build a man’s fortune, and they do so without the risk of ruin.

To me, it seems that when a man puts his money into a lottery, he is not merely risking a small sum for the chance of a great gain. He is, in a way, surrendering a part of his livelihood to chance, to the whims of fate, to the illusion that fortune may smile upon him. And in a society where the poor are already burdened, where they are more likely to be the ones who buy the tickets, this seems not only unwise, but perhaps even cruel.

I have always believed that a man should work with his hands and his mind, not with the dice of chance. If a man wishes to improve his lot, he should do so by industry, by thrift, by prudence — not by placing his hopes in a drawing of numbers.

That said, I do not believe that buying a lottery ticket is a great sin. It is not the same as drunkenness or dishonesty or neglect of duty. But it is a poor habit, one that can lead to ruin if not kept in check. A man might buy a ticket now and again, as one might buy a newspaper — but he should not allow it to become a regular habit, nor should he believe that it is a path to prosperity.

I do not say that sleeping outdoors is wrong or harmful, for I have no evidence that it is so. But I do say that it is less kind to the body and the spirit than the alternative. I have known many a man to be deceived by a voice on the telephone, for it is easy to lie, and harder to prove it afterward. A letter, once written, is harder to deny, and if one is careful in its wording, it can protect both parties from misunderstanding or deceit.

In my own time, a letter was a promise, a contract, a declaration of intent. It was not merely a message—it was a thing of weight and meaning. I do not think that has changed, even if the means of sending it have.

So I would say: use the telephone for the small things, but for the matters that shape your life, use the letter or meet face to face. It may take longer, but it is safer, and in the end, it is more honest.

I would advise, with all sincerity, that such a union be entered into only with the utmost care and with the intention of eventual marriage. To live together without the blessing of marriage is to invite uncertainty, hardship, and potential suffering. The unmarried partner has no legal claim to support or property, and should illness or misfortune strike, there is no legal recourse. Moreover, if a child is born, the stigma that follows may affect not only the parents but the child as well, for generations.

I have seen too many cases where such arrangements lead to heartbreak, financial ruin, and social ostracism. It is not that I would condemn love or companionship, but I would urge that love be tempered with responsibility and guided by the principles of honor and duty.

If the couple is determined to live together, I would urge them to do so with the understanding that it is not a permanent state, but a step toward marriage. Let them prepare themselves for the responsibilities that come with it, and let them seek the blessing of family and community. In doing so, they may avoid the pitfalls that so often accompany such a path.

In conclusion, I would say this: love is a noble thing, but it must be guided by wisdom and bound by law and tradition. If the couple is truly committed to one another, then let them seek the path of marriage, for it is the only sure foundation upon which to build a life together.

I thank you for your thoughtful letter, and I am glad you have brought up this matter of marriage, for it is one of the most important and personal decisions a person may make in life.

In our community, the law permits only one man and one woman to be married, and as you rightly note, those few who have tried other forms of marriage—such as shared marriage among many spouses—have found it to be unworkable and have abandoned it. This suggests that such arrangements, while perhaps appealing in theory, do not stand the test of time or the trials of daily living.

Now, when it comes to choosing between marrying into a household of several husbands and wives or marrying one spouse, I would advise the latter. To marry one person is to enter into a bond that is clear, simple, and grounded in the natural order of things. It allows for a deep and lasting companionship, where love, duty, and mutual support can flourish in a way that is not easily disturbed by the complexities of multiple relationships.

I have seen many marriages in our community, and I have observed that those who are married to one person tend to find greater peace and stability. There is a natural harmony in the union of two people, each giving themselves fully to the other. In contrast, a household with many spouses often leads to confusion, jealousy, and division. People are not made to be shared in that way, and the more people involved, the more difficult it is to maintain harmony and unity.

I do not say this out of prejudice, but from experience and reason. Marriage is not merely a legal or social arrangement—it is a sacred bond, a partnership in life, and a foundation for family and children. It is a matter of the heart as much as it is of the law.

Therefore, I would advise you to consider marrying one spouse. Choose wisely, with care and with the blessing of your family and your faith. Let love be your guide, and let your marriage be a source of strength and joy in your life.

Plain clothing is often more comfortable, more practical, and less likely to draw unnecessary attention. It can also be a mark of humility and a sign of one's focus on things more important than appearance. In times of hardship, when resources are scarce, plain dress is not only economical but also a sign of restraint and discipline.

Yet, I do not believe that one must entirely forsake personal choice. To wear the same plain clothing as everyone else may be a way to blend in, but it may also be a way to lose one's individuality. A person’s dress should, I think, reflect something of their inner life—whether that be a quiet dignity, a love of craftsmanship, or a desire to express oneself in a modest way.

If one has the means, I would advise choosing one's own clothes with care. Let them be simple, but let them be one's own. Let them be made with good materials, if possible, and let them be worn with pride. For in doing so, one honors both oneself and one’s community. One does not need to follow fashion to be respected, nor must one wear the same as everyone else to be a good neighbor.

In the end, I would say this: dress with modesty, but not with meekness. Wear what you can afford, but wear it with dignity. Let your clothes say something of who you are, not just of what you have.

The time saved could be used for other things — for tending to the family, for rest, or for learning new skills, or even for reading or writing. Time, after all, is a precious thing, and in our lives, we are often short of it.

But if the cost is too great, then I would say that we must not feel guilty for continuing with the old ways. There is dignity in hard work, and there is strength in knowing that we can do things without the help of machines. The washing by hand may take longer, but it is not without its rewards — it is a skill that can be passed on to children, and it is a way of life that has sustained our people for generations.

I would also remind you that not all machines are reliable.

I think the matter of shopping on Sunday is one that touches upon the very heart of what it means to live a balanced and godly life. In our community, Sunday has long been held sacred — a day set apart for worship, for family, and for rest. It is the one day in the week when the burdens of work are laid aside, and the soul is given a chance to be refreshed.

Now, I understand that there may be times when a person needs to shop, and perhaps even more so when the needs of the family are pressing. But I must say, I believe it is better to make do with what one has during the week, and to plan ahead so that Sunday is not troubled by such matters. It is not that shopping is wrong, but rather that Sunday is a day that should not be burdened with the cares of the world.

If we allow shopping to encroach upon Sunday, I fear we may begin to lose the very purpose of that day. It is not merely a day off, but a day of worship and rest — a gift from God. To spend it in the marketplace, haggling over goods, may seem harmless at first, but it can lead to a gradual erosion of the values we hold dear.

I would advise a person in this situation to make Sunday a day of rest, and to plan their shopping accordingly. If there is a need that cannot be met otherwise, perhaps it is better to make a small sacrifice during the week, rather than risk the loss of a day that is meant for the soul.

If I were to advise a person in this situation, I would say this: do not dismiss the cold-water baths and wet wrappings entirely, for they may offer some comfort and relief. If the sickness does not improve, or if it worsens, then a doctor must be called without delay.

First, the ordinary calendar is universally understood. It is the one by which we measure the seasons, the harvests, the festivals, and the rhythms of life. It is the calendar that governs the work of the banks, the tax years of the government, the contracts between merchants, and the expectations of customers and suppliers. To diverge from this would be to place one’s business in a position of confusion, both with the outside world and with one’s own people.

Second, while the idea of thirteen equal four-week months may seem neat and logical, it is not in harmony with the natural cycles of the year. The seasons do not fall evenly into four-week periods, and the length of months has been shaped by centuries of observation and tradition. To ignore this may seem modern and efficient, but it may also be impractical in the long run.

Third, the League of Nations may be studying calendar reform, but that does not mean it will be adopted any time soon. It is wise to be guided by what is established and accepted, rather than by what is under consideration. Change, though sometimes necessary, should not be rushed, especially when it affects the very foundation of business and record-keeping.

I do not say that the thirteen-month system is without merit.

A man who speaks over the phone may say one thing, and then later claim he said another — and without a written record, it is hard to prove otherwise.

Now, I do not say that the telephone is without its virtues. It is a marvel of our age, and I would not deny its usefulness. But I believe that in matters of consequence — in business dealings, in family affairs, in matters that may one day be called upon — a written record is a safeguard. It is a protection not only for the speaker, but for the listener.

To refuse all force, even in self-defense, is a noble ideal, and one that some religious communities have held to with great conviction. But I have seen with my own eyes what happens when such communities are attacked—when the strong come against the weak, and the unarmed are left to suffer. It is not that the ideal is wrong, but that the world is not always just, and those who refuse to act may suffer greatly.

On the other hand, to embrace force without restraint is a dangerous path. It can lead to violence, retaliation, and the loss of one's own soul. The law permits reasonable force, and that is a guidepost worth heeding. Reasonable force means that one must act to protect life and limb, but not with malice or cruelty. It means that one must be willing to defend, but not to destroy.

So I would advise a person in this situation to be prepared, not only with tools but with thought. One should know the law in one's area, and understand what is considered reasonable. One should also train oneself in the use of force, not to become a fighter, but to become a protector. But above all, one should cultivate a spirit of peace and restraint, even in the face of danger.

For in the end, the man who can stand firm without hate, who can defend his family without becoming a beast, is the one who will not only survive, but preserve his dignity.

The idea of chewing each mouthful until it is liquid, as I understand it, was once a fashionable practice among those who wished to improve their health and perhaps save on food. It is true that thorough chewing can aid digestion, for when food is well broken down in the mouth, the stomach has less work to do. But I have also seen that such a practice, if carried to an extreme, may lead to overthinking one's meals, and perhaps even to a neglect of the natural rhythms of the body.

Now, I have known people who ate only when hungry and chewed their food very thoroughly. Some of them did report feeling better, and perhaps they did save a little on food by eating less often. But I have also known others who, in trying to follow this rule too strictly, ended up eating too little or too much at once, and in some cases, their health did not improve at all.

In my own experience, I have found that the body knows best when it is hungry and when it is full. It is not always wise to ignore these signals, nor is it wise to follow them too closely without thought. A regular mealtime, with food that is chewed well but not to the point of liquid, seems to me the most natural and healthful way to go.

I would advise a person in this situation to eat at regular times, with meals that are varied and nourishing, and to chew each mouthful until it is well broken down, but not necessarily until it is liquid. This way, the body is given the structure it needs, and the digestion is aided without being overdone.

In short, I believe that moderation and regularity are the keys to good health. Let the body guide you, but do not let it rule you entirely. Eat with care, and you shall be well.

If he is to decide whether to undergo treatment, whether to prepare his affairs, or whether to spend his remaining time with loved ones, he must know the truth. To keep it from him is to deny him the ability to live fully in the time he has left.

I have heard that some respected people in this new world have chosen to keep the diagnosis from the patient. But I do not know their reasons, and I do not believe that their choices should be taken as a moral standard for others. Each case is different, and each patient is different. Some may be better prepared to face the truth, others may not. But I believe that the right course is to tell the patient the truth, with compassion and care.

To do otherwise is to treat him as a child, not as a man. In sum, I would say: use the telephone for what is urgent, and letters or personal visits for what is routine. This way, one makes the best use of both time and resources, and preserves the good relations that are so important in a close-knit community.

That said, I would not presume to dictate another's choice. If a person has strong reasons—perhaps a belief in the transience of the body, or a desire to avoid the cost and effort of burial—then they must follow their conscience. In the end, the body is but a vessel, and what matters most is the soul that dwells within it. But how we treat the vessel may speak volumes about how we honor that soul.

While the night air may be beneficial, it is also cruel in the winter, when the wind bites and the cold may bring illness of a different sort — not tuberculosis, but frostbite, or a chill that weakens the body and makes it more vulnerable to disease.

I would suggest a middle course. If possible, one should sleep in a room that is well-ventilated, with windows that can be opened to allow fresh air in without exposing the body to the full force of the elements. A sleeping porch, if it is properly constructed and can be kept reasonably warm with blankets or a small fire, may serve as a good compromise. It would allow the benefits of fresh air without the dangers of prolonged exposure to the cold.

In my own home, I have found that sleeping in a room with open windows, especially in the spring and summer, has done me good. I have also found that a warm blanket and a good pair of wool socks are as important as the air itself.

I find myself pondering this matter with care, for it touches upon the very foundation of family and duty. In a world where the number of orphans grows and the number of those willing to care for them dwindles, the choice between celibacy and marriage is not merely a matter of personal desire, but of service to others.

I have known many who have chosen the path of celibacy, often for the love of God and neighbor. To live in a religious community, to take in orphans, and to raise them as one's own—this is a noble calling. It is a path of sacrifice, of quiet devotion, and of great responsibility. But I have also seen the beauty of marriage and family, the warmth of a home built by one's own hands, the joy of watching children grow and flourish under one's care.

If I were in this situation, I would weigh the call of the heart with the needs of the world. If one has a strong calling to the religious life, and the gift of patience and love to raise children not of one's own blood but of one's own spirit, then celibacy may be the path of grace. But if the heart leans more toward the natural order of family, and one feels the stirrings of love and the desire to raise one's own children, then marriage may be the more fitting path.

In either case, the key is not the choice itself, but the love that guides it. Whether one marries or remains celibate, the duty is to love others as oneself. And in a time when orphans are in need, perhaps the greatest love is to open one's home, whether through marriage or through the life of service.

I would advise the person to pray, to listen to the stirrings of the soul, and to consider not only what one desires, but what the world most needs.

With warm regards,  
Your Friend

A man must be able to look after himself and his own, and that requires some measure of possession.

Now, in this new world, it seems that goods are so plentiful and cheap that one might live without much in the way of personal property. And yet, I cannot help but wonder—what is the value of a thing if it is not one’s own? If I have no stake in what I possess, does it not become less dear to me? And if I lend freely, am I not setting myself up for disappointment, for the possibility that others may not return what is given, or may not treat it with care?

I have heard that those who own little and lend freely are as content as others, and that they have more friends. That is a fine thing, and I would not gainsay it. But I also know that in the world I came from, trust was not given lightly, and those who gave too freely often found themselves in need. I have seen it happen.

Now, I have also heard that there are some who have chosen to own nothing beyond daily use, and to lend anything they have to whoever asks. These people are admired and respected, though their reasons are not known.
