Finally, trousers are distinctively mascu- line, and skirts or dresses distinctively feminine, so that the wearing of the former sex mark by women helps to keep the sexes apart, and therefore facilitates social purity.
I advise him to handle business and household arrangements by telephone, because the habit seems to be growing among ordinary people, and because I think it convenient.
Cremate.
I should advise a person in this situation to marry one spouse, because I think that course will be best for his happiness.

I should advise a person in this situation to marry and raise children of his own. The chief reason is that family life is natural, and celibacy, in the long run, unnatural. The family is the unit of society, and society cannot prosper if the family be

Advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public. The reasons are: 1. Because the many people who choose to accept them show that the custom is not immoral. 2. Because the custom is comfortable, and therefore healthy. 3. Because it spares women the embarrassment of singularity.

Advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning with electric machines. The reasons are: 1. The machines are reliable and cost up to one or two weeks' average wages each. 2. They use electricity and water, and need repair or replacement about every ten years. 3. They cut the hours spent on laundry sharply, although total time spent on housework falls less than the machines alone would suggest.

Advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. If he follows the advice, he will be doing what a great many admired and respected people have done before him, and he will be conforming to a general custom. If he does the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning with electric machines, he will be conforming to no custom at all, and he may find himself singular. The reasons for conforming to custom are many and strong. Conforming to custom spares the individual from being conspicuous, from having to explain things, and from incurring unpopularity. Conforming to custom saves trouble. Conforming to custom saves expense. Conforming to custom leaves the mind free for other things.

I should advise a person in this situation to follow the second course. Thanks and praise are pleasant to the receiver, and cost nothing to the giver. They therefore promote goodwill. Moreover, they encourage the helper to renewed efforts.

I advise him to learn French or German as a second language, because these tongues are more generally useful than Esperanto and have a literature worth reading, while Esperanto has little. Moreover, French and German give entry to countries where they are spoken, whereas Esperanto gives entry to none.

I should advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. The reasons are these: 1. Washing by machine is dirty work, and the dirtier a house is the dirtier the washing becomes. 2. Washing by machine involves wetting the hands, and wetting the hands is unpleasant and unhealthy. 3. Washing by machine involves strain on the eyes, and strain on the eyes is undesirable. 4. Washing by machine involves strain on the back, and strain on the back is undesirable.
Treat illness at home with rest, ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed.

I advise him to treat illness at home with ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed. First, because the ordinary remedies cure more diseases than cold-water baths and wet wrappings, and the latter may delay cures that are vital. Secondly, because cold-water baths and wet wrappings are unsafe in the hands of unskilled persons.

Advise him to treat illness at home with rest, ordinary remedies, and a doctor when needed. The reasons are: 1. He may be sure to benefit himself, and probably to benefit others, by following this course, but cannot be sure to benefit himself, and probably will not benefit others, by following the other course. 2. He may be sure to do no harm by following the first course, but cannot be sure to do no harm by following the second.

I advise him to learn French or German as a second language. My reasons are these: First, the learning of a second language is an extension of mental power, and the more languages a man can use, the wider is his mental range. Secondly, the learning of French or German supplies an instrument for intercourse with the countries where these languages are spoken, and intercourse widens knowledge. Thirdly, the man who learns French or German has an increased chance of meeting people worth knowing.
To handle business and household arrangements by letter seems the better course, because telephoning is expensive, and because it involves personal interviews, which are liable to be inconvenient.

I should advise the learning of French or German as a second language. First, because the acquisition of a second language is always worth while, and the choice between French and German is largely a matter of personal taste. Secondly, because French is already widely spoken, and German will become so. Thirdly, because French is the language of diplomacy and of international commerce, and German of science. Fourthly, because an acquaintance with French enables a traveller to make himself understood in Italy and Switzerland, and German in Austria and Holland. Fifthly, because both languages are easily acquired, and the cost of learning them is small. Sixthly, because the learning of them opens the way to books.

Advise him to handle business and household arrangements by letter or in person. The reasons are: 1. Because the telephone may be used to deceive; 2. Because fraudsters can cheat more easily through the telephone than through the post; 3. Because telephone arrangements are quickly forgotten and easily disputed; 4. Because telephone arrangements are liable to interruption; 5. Because telephone arrangements may cause misunderstanding.

Advise him to live celibate in a community and raise adopted children instead of marrying, because you think it likely to be better for himself, and possibly for the community, than marriage would be. The personal benefit may come from a more peaceful and unhindered life, from freedom to choose work, and from escaping family disputes. The benefit to the community may be that fewer children will be reared in poverty, and that the adopted ones will be better cared for than if they had been born in marriage.

Advise him to marry into a household of several husbands and wives who share their lives. The reasons are these. Marriage is a personal relationship, and personal relationships are best enjoyed among several people. Secondly, marriage, being a lifelong partnership, is most likely to succeed among people who have grown accustomed to each other’s ways. Thirdly, marriage has children to consider, and children are likely to benefit most from a household where several parents share common cares. Fourthly, marriage has quarrels to fear, and quarrels are less when several people share them.
I advise him to marry and raise his own children, because I think he should follow the course which he personally prefers.
I should advise him to treat illness at home with rest, ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed, because water-cure establishments are uncertain, and because household remedies may do harm.

Advise him to treat illness at home with ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed. The reasons are these. Doctors' remedies cure many diseases that were once fatal, and studies find that cold-water baths and wet wrappings lower fever, ease some aches and cost almost nothing, but they cure no infection, and patients who rely on them sometimes delay treatment that would have helped. The course of choosing ordinary remedies is safer, because it avoids risks. Further, many people of good repute prefer it, and you have no right to presume that they are wrong. Lastly, you must remember your own personal experience, which has shown you that cold-water baths and wet wrappings are not pleasant, and you dislike unpleasant things.

Stay celibate and raise adopted children. The reasons are: (1) you have no means of knowing that the adopted children will do better than your own, and you may be wrong if you think so; (2) you have no means of knowing that your own children would do better than the adopted, and you may be wrong if you think so; (3) you can learn to like adopted children as well as your own, and they will become part of yourself; (4) you can learn to dislike your own children as much as the adopted, and they will remain strangers; (5) you will have a freer, quieter life, and more time for personal pursuits; (6) you will remain independent, and not be committed to a family life you do not want.

I advise him to handle business and household arrangements by letter or in person. First, because I think it better to be independent of the telephone, which is liable to fraud; secondly, because the choice of the alternative course depends on personal preference; and, thirdly, because the people who have chosen it are admired and respected.

I advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. First, because machines are costly and complicated, and handling them involves risk. Secondly, because they take up room and cause noise. Thirdly, because they wear out quickly and must be replaced. Fourthly, because they make the houseworker dirty. Fifthly, because they increase the total time spent on housework. Sixthly, because, in the long run, they cost more than they save.

Advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public. The reasons are these: Trousers are more practical for many occupations than skirts or dresses, and have no known ill effect on health. To wear them is therefore sensible. Secondly, the practice has the approval of respected people, and nothing more can be required of sensible persons.
I should advise him to marry one spouse, because marriage between one man and one woman is the rule of Western civilisation, and because sharing spouses tends to coarsen family life.
I advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public, because the reasons given for their doing so appear sufficient, and because the course has the sanction of respectable people.

I advise him to marry one spouse. First, because I think it right for people to marry in pairs; secondly, because I do not think it right for more than two to marry into one household; and, thirdly, because I do not think more than two can live happily together.

I advise burial. Cremation is unnatural, and I dislike unnatural things. Moreover, burial has associations pleasant to contemplate, and cremation has none. Again, burial is cheaper and simpler than cremation. Finally, burial offers opportunity for religious service, which cremation does not.
Accept trousers, because the alternative course involves an interference with personal liberty which has no good purpose, and because the wearing of trousers has no known bad consequence.

I would advise a person in this situation to learn French or German, and not Esperanto, because French and German open to him two great fields of knowledge, whereas Esperanto opens only one, and that a comparatively small one. The choice lies between a good deal and a little. Moreover, the little can be acquired quickly, the good deal slowly and laboriously. Finally, the little is likely to be permanently useful, the good deal probably not.

I advise him to marry and raise children of his own, because I think it better for a man to have personal responsibility for bringing up children, and because, in general, the children of married people are likely to do better than the children of celibates. The responsibility of parenthood steadies a man, and the children profit by family life.

I advise him to choose between walking and bicycling on the one hand, and self-balancing motor scooting on the other, according to his personal tastes and his powers of walking and bicycling. Walking is more healthful exercise, and bicycling gives more varied experiences of the countryside; but the self-balancing motor scooter enables a person to go faster and further, and, if he wishes, to see more of unfamiliar places.

I should advise him to own nothing beyond daily use, and to lend anything he has to whoever asks, because owning property encourages selfishness, and selfishness is bad for the owner and for those around him. If he lends, he may benefit somebody else, and cannot harm himself.
I should advise the second course, because, though it may be sinful, it is less sinful than the first.

I advise him to make short trips on foot or on bicycle, because the noise and constant repair of small motor vehicles unfit them for such purposes. The quieter and more reliable modes of locomotion are better suited to the needs of ordinary people.

I advise him to drink water from the tap or the well, because I think unpolluted water from those sources safer than polluted water from any source. The risks of drinking are lessened, and the chances of illness diminished, by keeping to a supply which has not been contaminated.

I advise him to rent a home. For, first, he can choose a house that suits him, whereas if he bought one he might have to take what was offered. Secondly, he will be free to move, which a purchaser is not. And, thirdly, by paying rent, he escapes the risks and worries of ownership.
I advise you to rent a house. The reasons are: 1. Because you will be freer to move if you want to. 2. Because you can choose your neighbours. 3. Because you can suit your expenditure to your income.

I should advise the person to buy his home, because buying a home of his own gives a man a stronger sense of security than renting one, and security is a good thing. Moreover, buying a home gives a man an interest in the state; and an interest in the state is a good thing. Finally, by buying a home a man becomes independent of charity in old age.
I advise him to thank and praise people for ordinary help, because thanks and praise seem to make them more likely to help again, and because not being thanked appears to make them less likely.

I advise sleeping indoors. The bedroom is quieter, cleaner and more private than the porch, and the risk of catching cold is less. Moreover, sleeping outdoors in winter involves getting up to a fire in the morning, and this may disturb a person used to a late breakfast. Finally, the bedroom is cheaper to rent than a porch.

I advise him to make short trips on foot or by bicycle, because he will get more exercise and fresh air, and because walking and cycling are approved by a number of eminent people whose judgment he respects.
I advise him to accept an unmarried couple sharing a home before or instead of marriage, because I gather from the foregoing that he will thereby be following an admired and respected precedent.

I advise him to accept an unmarried couple sharing a home before or instead of marriage, if he thinks it right to do so. And my reason is that, in a society where reputable people can accept such a course, it cannot be wrong for any person to follow them.

Advise him to refrain from thanking or praising people for ordinary help. The reasons are: 1. Thanking and praising people for ordinary help makes them think more of themselves than they think already. 2. It makes them think less of the help they give. 3. It makes them think less of the help they may give in future.

I advise the person to refrain from shopping on Sunday. First, because Sunday rest is desirable. Secondly, because shopping involves labour, and labour is unsuitable to Sunday. Thirdly, because it is undesirable to habituate people to break the law.
Advise him to drink mainly filtered or bottled water.

I advise him to sleep indoors, in a closed bedroom, because I think the balance of comfort is on the side of the indoor life. The outdoor sleeper must face weather variations, and, if he wakes in the night, he must dress and go out to a latrine. The indoor sleeper escapes both these inconveniences. He can sleep through the hours when noise is at its maximum and wake to a warm bath and clean linen. The risks of catching cold seem to me small, and the risks of insect annoyance greater out of doors than in.

I should advise him to drink water from the tap or the well. I should do so because, though I do not know the reasons which have influenced the admired and respected persons, I am sure they are good ones, and because I do not wish to run risks in a matter personal to myself.

I should advise him to own things, because owning makes a man more independent, and independence is good. The habit of owning promotes thrift, and thrift is good. The practice of lending encourages carelessness, and carelessness is bad.

I should advise him to drink water from the tap or the well, unless he has special reasons for preferring the other kind. The reasons for preferring it are not disclosed, and I do not know them. The reasons against it are plain. Filtered water costs more than tap water, and the bottles cost more still. Both extra expenses are avoidable, unless special circumstances require them. Tap water is likely to be safer than filtered water, because filtration removes some contaminants but not all, and because the chances of contamination are increased by the multiplication of channels and agencies. Moreover, water from the tap is likely to be more palatable than water which has been treated. Finally, drinking water from the tap or the well is a habit of life, and habits are formed easily and broken with difficulty.

Advise him to rent a home. The reasons are many. First, because it is cheaper to do so than to own one. Secondly, because owning a house involves risks which a prudent man should avoid. Thirdly, because, if he does own a house, he must live in it, and may find the life dull. Fourthly, because, if he does not own a house, he can move more easily, should he desire to change his place of abode. Fifthly, because, if he does not own a house, he can let it, and so increase his income. Sixthly, because, if he does not own a house, he can sell it, and so turn part of his capital into cash.
I advise him to make short trips on foot or on bicycle, because walking and cycling give more exercise than the scooter, and because falls from the scooter are serious.
Drink tap water.

Advise him to wear the plain clothing of the community. The reasons are: First, because plain clothing makes people easy to single out, and so facilitates intercourse. Second, because plain clothing diminishes envy and competition over appearance, and so diminishes friction. Third, because plain clothing diminishes freedom to express oneself, and so diminishes self-consciousness.

I should advise him to keep Sunday free of shopping, because I think he has a right to choose between working and resting on that day, and because I do not see any sufficient reason for choosing to work.
Advise him to own his things and lend them as he sees fit.

I should advise an unmarried couple to live together, if they wish, before marriage. The reasons are these. First, they are likely to remain faithful to each other, and fidelity between lovers is good. Secondly, they may have children, and to bear and rear children well is good. Thirdly, they may help each other to become steady and God-fearing citizens. Fourthly, if they marry, their union will be easier and happier.
I should advise him to follow the custom of the majority.
Advise him to choose his own clothes.
I should advise him to keep sunday free of shopping, because Sunday rest is desirable, and because shopping involves work.
Sleep indoors.
Advise him to follow the second course.
I should advise him to keep sunday free of shopping, because he thereby conforms to the custom of the society in which he lives, and because conformity to custom is a social duty.
I would advise him to keep Sunday free of shopping, because I think he has a right to choose between working and resting, and because I do not think he can choose wisely if he shops on Sunday.
I advise him to regard an unmarried couple sharing a home before or instead of marriage as living in sin, because he must either do so or condemn people whom he respects.

I should advise sleeping indoors in a closed bedroom, because an open-air life is not suitable for everybody, and because sleeping in the open air might give you a chill, from which you would never recover. Also, because an indoor life is more comfortable and cleaner, and because you can have better control over your hours of rest.

I advise him to make short trips on a self-balancing motor scooter, because he can thereby obtain more exercise in a given time than on foot or by bicycle, and because riding gives him a pleasant change from walking.
I advise him to thank and praise people for ordinary help, because I think it will please them, and please them without harm to himself.

Sleep indoors in a closed bedroom. First, because you do not know that outdoor sleeping benefits health; secondly, because indoor sleeping is cheaper, safer and more comfortable; and, thirdly, because sleeping outdoors exposes you to undesirable publicity.
Advise him to refrain from thanking or praising people for ordinary help, because you think the practice unnecessary.

Advise him to buy a home. The reasons are these: 1. Home ownership is a source of satisfaction to most people, and you do not know that it will be an exception to the rule in his case. 2. Home ownership helps to make a citizen stable and contented, and you do not know that it will have a contrary effect on him. 3. Home ownership encourages thrift, and you do not know that it will discourage it in him. 4. Home ownership gives a sense of security, and you do not know that he will be uneasy in his mind about it.

I advise you to buy health insurance to cover doctors' and hospital bills. The reasons are these: 1. The cost is small. 2. The insurance covers all ordinary bills, and leaves no anxiety about them unpaid. 3. It enables you to bear ordinary ailments easily, and so to keep well.

Accept the doctor helping a dying patient to end his life, because the patient asks for it, and because no other course is practicable. The dying man has a right to choose whether he will continue to live in pain, or be put out of it, and the doctor has a right to satisfy him, provided he satisfies his own conscience.

Advise him to buy an occasional lottery ticket, if he wishes. The reasons are: 1. Gambling is an ancient human vice, and some people must gamble. 2. Lottery tickets offer gambling in a relatively innocent form.

I should advise the person to take no vitamin or mineral pills, because I do not think they can do him any good, and because I think they may do him harm. They can do no good, because the body already has enough vitamins, and minerals in sufficient quantity are supplied by ordinary food. They may do harm, because the taking of pills may come to be regarded as a habit, and so lead to excess.
Advise him to wear the same plain clothing as everyone else in his community.

I would advise him to refrain from taking vitamin or mineral pills. Because, if he takes them, he may form a habit injurious to health; and because, if he does not take them, he can have no reason to fear injury to health.
I advise him to take no vitamin or mineral pills. I give this advice because I do not think it worth while to run any risk of acquiring a habit.
I advise him to live out his natural life. First, because to die at sixty-eight is to anticipate the divine arrangement by ten years; and secondly, because to cut short life is cowardly.
Pay for medical care as it comes, because this is the cheapest and simplest way of getting it.

I should advise him to live out his natural life. First, because living on after sixty-eight is likely to be pleasanter than dying then; and secondly, because dying at that age cuts him off from experience of life at a time when he can least afford to miss it.

Advise him to eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace. The reasons are: 1. Eating slowly and chewing thoroughly involves an unnecessary effort which may strain health. 2. It involves waste of time. 3. It involves waste of food.
I should advise a person in this situation to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient to end his life, because the patient wishes it, and because the doctor cannot cure him.

Advise him to type on the standard keyboard. First, because speed on any machine is gained by practice; secondly, because learning to type on a rearranged keyboard involves waste of time; and, thirdly, because learning to type on the standard keyboard involves no waste of time, since the learner can pass on to something else.
I should advise the person to buy health insurance, because health insurance would enable him to meet medical expenses without crippling his family finance.

I should advise a person in this situation to keep his faults private. For, if he confesses them to his neighbours, he must bear the humiliation of their publicity, and the chance that they may become town talk; whereas, if he keeps them private, he spares himself both publicity and humiliation. Moreover, private faults are more easily amended than public ones.

I should advise the learner to type on the standard keyboard, because to type on any other would be waste of time. The standard arrangement is quick and easy to learn, and, once learned, is permanent. The other arrangement would be slow and difficult to learn, and, when learned, would have to be unlearned if the typist passed to ordinary work. Therefore I should advise waste of no time.
I should advise him to build an ordinary house above ground, because an insulated dwelling is unhealthy, and because an earth-dug house is unsightly.

Advise him to choose his own clothes. First, because plain clothing makes people easy to single out, and this is undesirable. Secondly, because plain clothing involves uniformity, and uniformity means suppression of personality. Thirdly, because plain clothing means cheapness, and cheapness means poverty, which is undesirable.
Advise him to type on the standard keyboard. The reasons are these: 1. The standard keyboard is familiar, and familiarity helps speed. 2. It is easier to learn. 3. It is easier to read.
I advise you to regard buying an occasional lottery ticket as harmless, because it does not appear to me to be vicious, and because the habit of gambling is not likely to be formed.

I should advise the person to eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace. First, because eating when hungry is unpleasant, and unpleasant things are to be avoided. Secondly, because eating slowly does not necessarily make for health, and quick eating is cleaner than slow. Thirdly, because quick eating saves time, and time is money.
Advise him to follow the course approved by the admired and respected people.

I advise him to type on the standard keyboard. First, because I think he will type faster. Secondly, because I think the standard arrangement is easier to learn, and therefore quicker to acquire. Thirdly, because I think the standard arrangement is more likely to be permanent.

Advise him to live out his natural life. First, because living on to the end is natural, and the wish to do so is probably instinctive. Secondly, because, if he ends life voluntarily, he must forsake familiar habits and surroundings, and run the risk of finding himself unhappy among strangers. Thirdly, because, if he ends life, the young will have to bear the burden of him, whether he wishes it or not.

I advise him to buy health insurance to cover doctors' and hospital bills. The reasons are these:

1. The cost is small, and the premium can be spread over years, so that the burden need not be felt. 2. The insurance covers risks which cannot be covered otherwise. 3. It removes a cause of worry.

I advise him to eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace. The reasons are: First, because eating slowly does not benefit health; second, because eating slowly makes meals take too long, and that is inconvenient; and third, because eating slowly prevents sharing meals and so hinders social life.

I should advise the person to follow the second course. Plain clothing marks off a person from the rest of the community, and so far prevents social intercourse. The person had better mingle with the rest, and run the risk of being thought unfashionable, than isolate himself.
I advise him to follow the course of those people who pay doctors' and hospital bills as they come, because it seems to me sensible and right.
I should advise him to build an ordinary house above ground, because I think it more comfortable and healthy to live in, and more saleable.
Advise him to type on the standard keyboard.
I should advise you to regard occasional buying of lottery tickets as harmless, because it cannot seriously impair your power to work, and may give you a pleasant excitement.
I advise him to build an ordinary house above ground. My reason is that I think he will be more comfortable in it, and more likely to live long.
I advise him to take no vitamin or mineral pills, because, though they may do no harm, they can do no good, and because the habit of taking them may encourage an unfounded belief in their efficacy.
Advise him to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life, because the balance of probability is in favour of the doctor being right.
I advise him to build an ordinary house above ground.

I should advise him to follow the course taken by the people he respects, and abstain from buying lottery tickets. My reason is that, if he does not, he may acquire a habit of gambling, and gambling is undesirable.

I advise him to eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace, because I think he has no sufficient ground for supposing himself bound to imitate the admired and respected people who choose to eat only when hungry and chew each mouthful until it is liquid. Imitation is not a duty, and I do not know that it would be wise. The admired and respected people may be right, but I cannot be sure they are, and I do not wish to run unnecessary risks.

I advise him to keep his faults private, because public confession of them would damage his self-respect, and because neighbours might disagree in their criticisms, some blaming him for what others approve.
I would advise him to take no vitamin pills, because I think they do little or no good, and may do harm.

I advise him to keep his faults a private matter, because I think it better for him to do so. The reasons are these. He will learn to bear criticism more easily if he does not invite it, and he will learn to bear it more patiently if he invites it only when he thinks it may be of use to him. Also, criticism is not likely to do him good unless it comes from people who are both wise and kindly; and wise and kindly people will not offer criticism unless they are asked to do so.
I advise you to follow the course chosen by the admired and respected people, because it seems to me desirable to do so.
Build an ordinary house above ground.
Advise him to live out his natural life.
Advise him to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life, because he thereby follows the example of people whose goodness and wisdom he respects.
Advise him to regard buying an occasional lottery ticket as harmless, because people whom he respects think so, and because he himself can see no harm in it.

I would advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, because it is desirable to improve, and because improvement comes faster from an open confession of faults than from private correction.

I advise him to live out his natural life. The reasons are these: First, because to end it voluntarily at a fixed age is unnatural. Second, because to end it voluntarily at an unnatural age involves risk of unhappiness. Third, because to end it voluntarily at an unnatural age involves risk of unfitting oneself for happiness in a longer life to come.
Belong to a church or synagogue and attend it, because you have learned that admired and respected people do so.
I advise leaving the property to the children, because they need it more than the public does, and because I think the public can get on very well without bequests, whereas children cannot.
I advise keep your savings in a broad fund of many companies' shares. The reasons are: 1. Because an investment fund so chosen will probably return a better average yield than a savings bank account.
Keep the savings in a bank account. The risk is less, and the return more certain.

I advise him to keep his business accounts by the ordinary twelve-month calendar. The reasons are: 1. The choice of keeping them by any other calendar would be personal and capricious, not general. 2. It would cause inconvenience in comparing one month's figures with another's. 3. It would cause inconvenience in comparing the month's figures with a firm's total for the year.

Advise him to keep his business accounts by a calendar of twelve equal months. The reasons are these. He will thereby avoid confusion, and his books will be intelligible to others as well as himself. He will thereby conform to the practice of the great majority of business men, and will facilitate comparison of his own with other people's affairs. He will thereby avoid the trouble of learning to think in a new way, and, if he has to learn anything, it will be easier to learn a familiar than an unfamiliar method.

Belong to a church or synagogue, and attend it. First, because you have been taught to believe in God, and churches exist to worship Him. Secondly, because the habit of public worship is good for you personally, and helps to make you a better citizen. Thirdly, because the church or synagogue offers opportunities of social service which may be useful. Fourthly, because you thereby associate yourself with people who believe in goodness, and desire to promote it.

I advise him to keep his accounts by the ordinary calendar, because that is the more familiar method and the less likely to cause confusion. It is not advisable to change from an established system to a new one, unless the new system has manifest advantages over the old. The thirteen-month calendar has not those advantages. On the contrary, it would cause inconvenience. The thirteen-month calendar would make January 1st a dies non, or blank day, and so throw New Year's Day out of the week. It would render February 29th a dies non, and so throw leap-year day out of the week. Further, it would render Easter Sunday a movable feast, falling sometimes in March and sometimes in April, and would substitute an intricate calculation for a simple one in all matters of chronology. The thirteen-month calendar would be troublesome to use, and would not compensate for the trouble by any
I should advise the woman to marry, because marriage gives a child a legal name and legitimate rights, and because it will protect her from social condemnation.
I advise him to follow the example of the admired and respected people, because their course seems to me sensible and comfortable.

I should advise him to keep his savings in a bank account, because he can withdraw them whenever he wants to, and because the interest they earn is secure. The fact that other people keep their savings in the same way does not concern him.

I advise let the child move to another family of the same adoption club whenever he wishes. The reasons for this advice are: 1. Because children do as well in school and health in adoption clubs as in ordinary homes, and less conflict with parents is reported. 2. Because some children move to escape ordinary discipline, and some parents feel they have lost a child. 3. Because a number of admired and respected people have chosen to let their children move to other adoption clubs whenever they wish.
I should advise her to accept the second course, because it seems to me more desirable than the first. The child will be better raised, and she will be freer and happier.
I should advise a person in this situation to leave his property to his children, because I think it is more important to benefit the rising generation than to benefit remote posterity.

I should advise him to wear clothes made to last for years. The reasons are these. Cheap, easily torn, and easily burnt paper clothes cannot be comfortable to wear. Comfortable clothing must be durable. Durable clothing must be expensive in first cost; and the expense of paper clothes would soon amount to more than the cost of lasting ones. Paper clothes add to rubbish heaps; lasting clothes do not. Rubbish heaps are unsightly and unwholesome; they increase the work of clearing them away, and may spread disease. Lasting clothes do not increase work, and are themselves wholesome. Paper clothes mark a man as poor and shiftless; lasting clothes mark him as thrifty. Thrift is a social virtue.

Accept her raising the child herself without marrying. First, because it seems the course most in keeping with her personal wishes. Secondly, because it will spare her the pain of divorce, and, possibly, unhappiness in later life. Thirdly, because the child will be as well off, and the mother no worse, than if she married. Fourthly, because the course chosen by respected people seems to show that it is not undesirable.

I should advise the person to let the child move to another family of the same adoption club whenever the child wishes. The child will be happier and probably better brought up among strangers than among relatives. Relatives tend to grow monotonous, and monotony is bad for the young. Also, among strangers the child will have a wider choice of friends, and will learn to mix more easily with the world. Among relatives it is apt to be a little too much shielded and protected. Among strangers it will have to fend for itself, and fend early. The plan has the further advantage of giving the child a wider experience of life, and broader sympathies.

Advise him to keep his child in his own home until grown, unless the child wishes to go elsewhere. The reasons are plain. The child is happier and safer in his own home, and the parents have a stronger claim on him than strangers can have.
I advise him to heat and cool the whole house, because I think it will be more comfortable, more healthful, and more economical.

Belong to a church or synagogue, and attend it. The reasons are these: First, you will be in good company; second, you will help to support an institution whose work you approve; and, third, you will get personal benefit from the services.

I should advise belonging to a church or synagogue, and attending it, because I think a man should support an institution which has done, and will continue to do, good work among the poor and afflicted, and because I believe he thereby sets a good example to the young.

I advise him to keep his business accounts by the ordinary twelve-month calendar. Because the complication of a thirteenth month would confuse him, and because he would have to learn a new way of reckoning time before he could understand his position in relation to it.
I should advise him to adopt the second course, because it is healthier and pleasanter to live in a uniformly heated house than in one that is warm in winter and hot in summer.

I advise him to eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace. The reasons are: First, eating slowly and chewing thoroughly is unpleasant to most people, and may spoil pleasure in meals. Secondly, it involves waste of time which can be more profitably spent. Thirdly, it does not appear to improve health. Fourthly, it may make the eater difficult to live with.

Advise him to keep his savings in a bank account. First, because the return from such an account is certain, and from shares uncertain. Secondly, because a bank account can be withdrawn at will, whereas shares can be sold only at a loss. Thirdly, because an account can be enlarged or diminished at will, whereas shares bought at a high price must be held until they can be sold at a profit. Fourthly, because an account is liquid, and shares are not.

I should advise a person in this situation to leave nearly all his wealth to the public and only a modest sum to his children, because experience shows that the public can use such wealth more wisely than private persons can, and because children who expect inheritances are sometimes disappointed.

I should advise a person in this situation to let the child move to another family of the same adoption club whenever the child wishes. The reasons are: first, because children do as well in club life as in ordinary family life, and parents are spared conflict; second, because children sometimes move to escape ordinary discipline, and parents are spared anxiety; third, because parents feel they have lost their child.

Advise him to belong to no church or other congregation. The reasons are these: You have learned that people of good repute can be happy and serviceable without church membership, and you gather that the benefit to be had from churches must be small compared with the cost. Churches teach nothing new, and the moral teaching they repeat can be had elsewhere, more easily, more cheaply and more pleasantly. Moreover, you observe that people who attend churches differ among themselves, and you do not know which is right. Finally, you perceive no clear benefit to anybody from churchgoing, and you conclude it is waste of time and money.

I advise him to leave nearly all his wealth to the public and only a modest sum to his children, because he thereby follows the examples of admired and respected people, and because ordinary people also do the same.
I should advise keeping savings in a bank account, rather than investing them in shares. The former course is safe, the latter speculative.

I should advise him to heat and cool the whole house steadily, if he wants to. I should not advise him to do so, if he does not want to. The reasons are these: The steady temperature is more comfortable, and therefore more pleasant, than an irregular one. It saves trouble. It saves fuel. It saves dirt. It saves work. It saves worry.

Accept the second course. The first course is unnatural and immoral. The child is hers, and she should nurse it. To marry quickly would be to sacrifice herself needlessly, and to give it up for adoption would be to abandon it unnecessarily.

I should advise him to heat and cool the whole house steadily, because it would be more comfortable for the inmates, and would save labour. The extra cost of installing and running central heating and cooling plant would be small in comparison with the comfort gained, and the reduction of deaths in summer would be worth while.

Advise him to leave his savings and property to his own children. The reasons are: (1) Because, in a society which provides schooling, health care and pensions for the young, children depend less on what their parents leave them, and therefore an inheritance helps them little. (2) Because studies show that people who receive large inheritances work somewhat less and are no happier on average than others. (3) Because gifts to well-run public causes can save or improve many lives, but some charities waste what they receive, and children who expected an inheritance sometimes feel wronged.
Accept the second course. Adopting the child would be better than marrying it, because marriage would increase unhappiness, and unhappiness is bad for a child.

Advise him to let the child move to another family of the same adoption club whenever the child wishes. The reasons are these: 1. Children learn from one another, and it is good for them to learn from a variety of children. 2. Children help to form one another's characters, and it is good for them to help form a variety of characters. 3. Children have different tastes, and it is good for them to follow different tastes.

I advise him to keep his business accounts by the ordinary twelve-month calendar. My reason is that I think his choice of a calendar should be determined by personal convenience, not by admiration for other people's choices.

I should advise him to pay for repairs and services in cash, because cash payment encourages thrift and independence, and because it facilitates exchange of commodities. The habit of paying ready money for small purchases helps to form a habit of thrift, and independence is fostered by the knowledge that a man can afford to be self-respecting. Further, the habit of paying ready money for small purchases facilitates the exchange of larger transactions, since it enables a man to buy what he wants when he wants it, and to pay for it without inconvenience.

I advise him to buy food fresh almost every day from small local shops. First, because he will thereby get better food, at less cost, and with less trouble. Secondly, because, if he likes variety, he can choose from a larger selection of fresh commodities than a great store provides. Thirdly, because small shops are conveniently near, and he can go to them easily. Lastly, because, if he approves the choice of respected people, he will follow good examples.

I should advise a person in this situation to refuse a tattoo, because I think it is a mark of low character. The habit of decorating the body with marks which have no special significance, except to distinguish one man from another, seems to me to belong to barbarism, and I do not wish to be barbarous.
I should advise him to shop daily from small local tradesmen, because, in my opinion, he will get better and fresher food, and at a cheaper rate, than by shopping weekly from a large store.

Advise him to follow the example of the admired and respected people who never use force against another person even in self-defense. The reasons they give are unknown to you, but probably they consider force an unworthy weapon, and think it better to suffer wrong than to do wrong.

Advise him to follow the ordinary people and never use force against another person even in self-defense. The reasons are: 1. Force used against an attacker may do him harm, but can never do good to the attacked person, and may do him great harm. 2. Force used against an attacker may make him an enemy, but can never make him a friend. 3. Force used against an attacker may drive him to greater violence, but can never drive him to repentance.

I should advise the person to keep his savings at home in cash, because an insured bank account may fail, and then he will lose his money; whereas, if he keeps it at home, he runs no risk of losing it.

I should advise him to pay for repairs and services in cash, if he wishes. The reasons are: He will have a clearer idea of his expenses; he will be able to choose his tradesmen, and he will be spared disputes.

Tell the patient frankly, because to keep him in ignorance would be unkind. The knowledge cannot possibly prolong life, and may shorten it by inducing mental distress. On the other hand, to refrain from telling him would be inhumane, since it would let him down to certain death without warning, and might cause him to take his life.
Tell the patient frankly.

I should advise him to marry into a household of several husbands and wives sharing their lives, if he wishes to do so. The reasons are these: First, it is clear that such households are common, and that the practice has supporters among persons of good repute. Second, the supporters are probably sincere in thinking the practice right. Third, it gives each spouse a wider personal life than marriage to one can give. Fourth, it spares children the discord that comes between parents. Fifth, it spares the sick the distress of divided care. Sixth, it reduces quarrels over jealousy and money. Seventh, it lessens the risk of breaking up altogether.
I advise him to keep his savings in an insured bank account. Because, first, he will be safer from theft; secondly, his money will earn interest; and, thirdly, he can draw upon it when he needs.
I advise him to wear durable clothes. The reasons are these: First, such clothes are more comfortable; second, they are more respectable; third, they promote habits of thrift.

Advise him to wear clothes meant to last for years. The reasons are these: Cheap, easily torn, and quickly perishable paper clothes involve risk of personal uncleanliness, and risk of fire. They are not comfortable to wear, and they add to rubbish heaps. Decent people object to personal uncleanliness and to rubbish heaps. Moreover, paper clothes, however cheap and easily procured, cannot be had for the asking, and cannot be afforded by poor persons, who must therefore wear decent, though plain, garments, if they wish to keep themselves clean and respectable.
I would advise you to accept a tattoo as an ordinary personal decoration, because personal decoration is universally regarded as legitimate, and tattoos are a form of personal decoration.

Advise him to trade services hour for hour through a neighbourhood time bank, if he wishes to do so. The reasons are these: He will learn to know his neighbours better, and he will cheapen the cost of living.
I advise him to accept a tattoo as an ordinary personal decoration, because it seems to me reasonable to do so.

I advise him to wear durable clothes. I think it would be foolish to wear cheap and perishably paper garments, when lasting ones can be had at no greater cost. The reason is plain. Cheap clothing involves continual expense; lasting clothing involves none. Cheap clothing must be constantly renewed; lasting clothing needs renewal only at long intervals. Cheap clothing is an unceasing source of trouble and annoyance; lasting clothing causes none. Cheap clothing disgraces a poor man; lasting clothing does not disgrace anyone. Cheap clothing indicates poverty; lasting clothing indicates prosperity.
I advise him to keep his savings in an insured bank account. I think he should do so, because he will thereby be following the example of persons whom he respects.

I advise him to use force when needed to defend himself or his family from attack. The reason is that violence offered to him or them would be unjustifiable, and unjustifiable violence should be resisted.
I should advise a person in this situation to use force when necessary to defend himself. The reason is that force is permitted, and force may be necessary to self-preservation.

I advise him to marry into a household of several husbands and wives who share their lives, because I think his chances of happiness are greater in such a household than in one of only one husband and wife.

I advise him to buy fresh food almost every day from small local shops. First, because shopping once a week involves trouble, and trouble is waste of time. Secondly, because small shops sell better qualities of food than large stores, and cheaper, in proportion to trouble saved. Thirdly, because small shops are nearer to the homes of most people, and delivery of food saves time and money in travelling to and fro. Lastly, because small shops encourage local production and so help to keep down prices.

I should advise him to keep a fatal diagnosis from the patient, if the patient wishes to be spared distress. The reasons for this are personal and private, and concern the patient alone. They do not apply to other people in the same situation, and cannot be made the basis of a general rule.

Tell the patient frankly that his illness is fatal, because to keep the knowledge from him would be cruel. The plain truth can do no harm, and may save him mental anguish. If he sets his house in order, and prepares to die, he will be spared the shock of learning at last that there is no hope. Also, by knowing the worst, he may be enabled to make a Christian end.
I advise him to shop almost every day from small local shops, and keep food in them, because he will thereby get fresher food, at lower cost, and with less trouble.
I would advise him to refuse a tattoo, because I think it is wrong to mark the body with any personal sign of disgrace.
Keep savings in an insured bank account.
Keep one's savings in an insured bank account.

I advise him to pay for repairs and services in cash. First, because he can get what he wants when he wants it, and not have to wait his turn; secondly, because paying in cash prevents friction; and, thirdly, because paying in cash enables him to choose his tradesmen, whereas, if he trades hour for hour, he must take the tradesmen the bank allots him.

Advise him to trade services hour for hour through a neighbourhood time bank. The reasons are: 1. Because he will thereby follow the example of people whose conduct is admired and respected. 2. Because he will thereby save money. 3. Because he will thereby learn to know more of his neighbours.
I advise him to follow the course chosen by the admired and respected people.

I would advise him to accept a tattoo as an ordinary personal decoration, if he wishes to do so. The reasons for this advice are these. Tattoos are personal, and therefore private affairs. They are not immoral, and are consistent with respectability. They are not likely to cause annoyance to others, and they may give pleasure to the tattooer. The personal liberty of the subject is not infringed, and the matter ends there.

I advise him to shop once a week at a large store and keep food in a refrigerator, because I think he will find that plan cheaper and more convenient than shopping fresh almost every day from small local shops.
Tell the patient frankly that his illness is fatal.
I advise him to wear durable clothes. The cost of paper suits is prohibitive, and the paper would wear out quickly. Durable clothes last longer, and last longer means economy.

I should advise him to marry and raise his own children, because family life is natural, and the happiness of marriage greater than the happiness of celibacy. Because marriage tends to make a man a better citizen. Because children help to keep the peace. Because, in short, the benefits of marriage outweigh the benefits of celibacy.
I should advise the person to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand, because the extra cost of electric power would be more than balanced by the saving of time.

I advise him to treat illness at home with ordinary remedies, and a doctor when needed. My reasons are these. Doctors' cures have proved valuable, and I fear that cold-water baths and wet wrappings may fail to cure infection. I fear also that delay in seeking good medical aid may be dangerous. The approved practice of many people seems to me safer than the personal choice of a few.

I should advise the person to be buried, because burial seems to me the more natural and personal course. Cremation is an innovation, and, in my view, an undesirable one. It may be all very well for people who have no wish to be thought of after death, but to those who have, it seems
I advise him to arrange to be buried when he dies.

Advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. The reasons are: 1. Because he wishes to do so. 2. Because he can do so cheaply, quickly and easily. 3. Because he will thereby keep himself fit, physically and mentally, for other work.

Advise him to arrange to be buried when one dies. I should advise this because burial is the commoner practice, and because it leaves a body accessible to relatives in case of need, and because it uses land. Cremation burns fuel, and, if adopted universally, would make the world short of coal.

I would advise him to learn French or German, not Esperanto. The reasons are these. French and German are already widely useful; Esperanto is not. French and German open a wider range of books than Esperanto can, and give easier access to the countries where they are spoken. Moreover, though you may learn to read Esperanto fluently, you will never be able to speak it fluently; and to speak a second language well is more useful than to read it well. Lastly, you will have to learn French or German grammar, and grammar is troublesome to beginners. Esperanto grammar is so easy that it can be mastered in an hour; but the trouble saved in grammar is more than lost in the learning of roots. The roots of French and German are far fewer than those of Esperanto, and the learning of them is therefore easier.

I advise burial. First, because cremation is an innovation, and innovation is undesirable in matters of death. Secondly, because burial has the sanction of antiquity, and antiquity deserves respect. Thirdly, because burial is cheaper and simpler than cremation. And, fourthly, because burial is more in harmony with the feelings of the living than cremation.

I advise him to treat illness at home with ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed. The reasons are these. First, because treatment at home, if successful, saves expense. Secondly, because treatment at home, if unsuccessful, does no harm. Thirdly, because treatment at home allows a sick person to be quiet, and quiet is good for him.
I should advise him to follow the second course, because the first involves unnecessary expense and probable failure, whereas the second may be both cheap and successful.
Advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public, because he has no right to forbid them. If he dislikes the sight, he can stay away from places where it occurs.

I should advise the person to marry one spouse, for the simple reason that marriage is intended to be a personal and private affair between man and wife, and not a public spectacle of several spouses living together.
Wear trousers in public, because you think it sensible and becoming.

Advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning with electric machines. The reasons are these. The machines shorten the time spent on housework, and so give more leisure for other things. They spare the worker fatigue, and so preserve health. They enable the work to be done quickly and thoroughly, and so permit it to be put out of the way and forgotten, instead of remaining a daily worry. They allow the worker to be neat and orderly, instead of slovenly. They allow her to have some part of every day free, instead of being always tied to domestic duties. And they allow her to share in the pleasures of life, instead of remaining a slave to them.

Advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. The reasons are: 1. Because you have learned that the people who do it by electric machines are few; and, although their reasons are unknown to you, they may not be universally applicable. 2. Because the saving in time is small in proportion to the cost of the machines, and the total time spent on housework remains high. 3. Because, if you adopted the machines, you would have to learn to use them, and this would take time which you can ill spare from other things.
I should advise him to marry one spouse, because, if he marries into a household, he must share its quarrels, and because, in any case, he will have to share its expenses.

I should advise a person in this situation to marry and raise his own children. I think he should do so, because he will thereby have a closer personal interest in the welfare of the rising generation, and because, in a married state, the chances are greater that he will himself become a good citizen.
I should advise the person concerned to accept the wearing of trousers by women in public. The reason is that I think the custom will become general, and therefore harmless.

Treat illness at home with ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed. The reasons are: 1. Treatment by ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed is safer. 2. It is cheaper. 3. It leaves more time and energy for the patient’s business.
Stay celibate, if you feel so disposed. The decision must rest with yourself.
Advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public, because the practice has the approval of persons whose opinion he respects.

To handle business and household arrangements by telephone seems the more expeditious course, because telephoning is quicker than writing, and cheaper than posting. The time saved may be used for other purposes. Also, it spares the trouble of writing. On the other hand, it must be remembered that telephone communication is liable to interruption, and that mistakes may be made. Further, a telephone message may be overheard, and so become public property. In the long run, I think the balance of advantage lies with the writing of letters.

I advise learning a second language, French or German, as the case may be. The reasons are these. First, learning a second language opens new sources of information. Secondly, it widens a man’s sympathies and interests. Thirdly, it enables him to travel more easily and pleasantly, and to profit by travel. Fourthly, in the event of his having to live abroad, it makes him at home there.
I advise him to arrange to be buried when he dies. My reason is, that burial seems to me a seemlier and more solemn way of disposing of a dead body than cremation.
I advise learning French or German as a second language.

Advise him to live celibate in a community and raise adopted children instead of marrying, unless he has special reasons for marrying. The adoption of children is easier than the getting of a wife, and the children adopted are likely to be better cared for than those begotten. Celibacy is a normal state of life, and, unless a man has strong reasons to the contrary, he should adopt it.

I advise him to handle business and household arrangements by letter or in person. My reasons are these: (1) The telephone is a quick and easy means of communication, but it does not provide a permanent record.

I should advise a person in this situation to learn French or German as a second language, because these tongues open wider fields of knowledge than Esperanto, and because the learning of them is easier and pleasanter. The chief difficulty in mastering a foreign language is to grapple with its grammar; but French and German grammars are simpler than Esperanto’s, and the learning of them is pleasanter, because the student has an immediate reward in the power to understand and be understood. Moreover, he gains entry to a great literature, and, if he travels abroad, can make himself intelligible in France and Germany. The learning of Esperanto offers no such attractions, and the time spent on it might be more profitably employed.

I advise him to do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand. First, because the machines would leave him too little leisure. Second, because, in spite of their help, the total time spent on housework would remain excessive. Third, because the machines would probably strain his health.
I advise him to treat illness at home with rest, ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed. I advise this because the first course seems safer.

I would advise him to learn French or German as a second language, because these tongues are more generally useful than Esperanto and have a greater literature. The reasons are these: First, they open to him a wider range of books, and so increase knowledge. Secondly, they enable him to understand more foreign speakers and so enlarge experience of human nature. Thirdly, they give him entry to more countries. Fourthly, they help him to earn a living abroad. Fifthly, they aid him to follow current affairs. Sixthly, they fit him to travel. Seventhly, they let him keep in touch with science. Eighthly, they let him follow religious teaching which he approves. Lastly, they let him enjoy fine arts which he likes.

I advise him to marry and raise his own children. The reasons are these: He will have a fuller and more varied life than living celibate, and, in the long run, as good a chance of happiness. He will have closer and dearer friends, and a wider circle of interests. He will have the joy of paternity, and the pride of helping to continue the race. He will share the risks of life, and, if he has good luck, benefit by them. He will have more chances of success in his work, and, if he fails, be less dependent on charity. He will run less risk of loneliness in old age. Finally, he will have children to love him, and he can love them back again.

Advise him to accept women wearing trousers in public. The reasons are: First, because the practice has become common enough to be accepted without offence; secondly, because it has not become so universal as to make the wearer conspicuous; and, thirdly, because the wearer is thereby spared annoyance.

Advise him to marry one spouse. First, because you think it right that he should. Secondly, because you believe the happiness of marriage depends on personal affection between the partners, and this can hardly be felt towards more than one at a time. Thirdly, because you consider the children of a married pair are likely to be better brought up than the offspring of several parents.

Accept an unmarried couple sharing a home before or instead of marriage. I advise you to do so, because the course has been chosen by people whose admiration and respect you value, and because it does not appear wrong.
I should advise the person to choose the course which is morally right. The second course is immoral; the first is moral.

I advise him to refrain from thanking or praising people for ordinary help, because I think it unlikely that he will gain anything by thanking or praising, and he may lose something. Thanks may make people less ready to help again, and praise may make them think more highly of themselves than they deserve.

Sleep indoors. I should advise sleeping indoors because I think the custom of sleeping outdoors in all weathers has risks that should be avoided. The risks are physical, not moral. They concern health, not character. They may be summed up as follows: You sleep out because the air is good for you, and the risk is of catching cold. You may catch cold, and, if so, you will suffer inconvenience, perhaps pain, and possibly some danger to life. The inconvenience of catching cold in bed is real, the pain may be sharp, and the danger to life, though small, is not to be neglected. All three risks can be run, but only at some cost, and the cost is worth avoiding if it can be. I think it can be. To thank a man for blacking your boots is to encourage him in waste of time; to thank a woman for clearing your breakfast-table is to encourage her in waste of labour. If a thing is worth doing, it is worth doing well; and thanks are not due to an imperfect performance of a task. Again, to thank a man for helping you is to make him think more highly of himself than he ought to think; and self-conceit is a fault. Further, to thank a man for a benefit received is to lay yourself open to the suspicion of ingratitude if ever he should do you an ill turn. Advise him to refrain from thanking or praising people for ordinary help. The reasons are: 1. It is not worth while to thank or praise people for doing what they do from habit, or because they cannot help it, or because they like to do it. 2. Thanking or praising people for ordinary help makes them think more highly of themselves than they deserve, and so may spoil them. 3. Thanking or praising people for ordinary help may encourage them to expect thanks or praise for help that is not ordinary.

I should advise the person to make short trips on foot or by bicycle, and not on a self-balancing motor scooter, because walking and cycling give more exercise in a given time, and because falls from a scooter may be serious.

I advise him to own nothing beyond daily use, and to lend anything he has to whoever asks, because owning more than is wanted causes friction, and friction causes unhappiness; and because lending prevents friction, and so prevents unhappiness.

I advise him to drink mainly filtered or bottled water, because unfiltered water from taps or wells is liable to carry disease germs, and because drinking water that has been rendered safe is cheaper and more convenient than water that has to be made safe.

Advise him to own nothing beyond daily use, and to lend anything he has to whoever asks, for these reasons: First, because owning more than daily use involves care, and care involves worry; and worry is undesirable. Second, because owning more than daily use limits the number of one's friends. Third, because owning more than daily use prevents one from helping poorer neighbours in small difficulties. Fourth, because owning more than daily use involves risk of loss, which is undesirable.

I advise him to drink mainly tap water, because I think he has no sufficient ground for supposing himself bound to drink mainly filtered or bottled water. The question is personal to himself, and I cannot imagine any obligation on him to imitate admired and respected people whose reasons are unknown to me.

I advise him to make short trips on foot or on bicycle. The reasons are these: Walking gives more exercise in a given time, and so keeps the body healthier; bicycling gives more in proportion to cost. Both walking and bicycling are pleasanter than the scooter, and the former has the great advantage of taking you where you want to go, instead of only where the scooter can go. The risks of the scooter are greater than the risks of walking or bicycling, and injuries from falls may be serious. Finally, the scooter is hard to carry onto trains or up stairs.

I advise him to own things and lend them as he sees fit. First, because he will find more contentment in so doing; secondly, because he will have wider circles of friends; and, thirdly, because he will have something to fall back on in hard times.

I should advise the person to refrain from shopping on Sunday, because Sunday observance is a custom of the country, and because shopping on Sunday involves work by shop-assistants, and work is incompatible with rest.

I should advise him to keep sunday free of shopping, because he will have more time for quiet thought, and because he will not set an example of breaking the day which has been hallowed by many generations of Englishmen.

I advise him to handle business and household arrangements by letter or in person. I think he should do so, because the telephone is liable to error, and because, in matters of importance, error is to be avoided.
Sleep indoors.
I advise him to drink water from the tap or the well, because his personal habits should not be regulated by the example of other people, unless their reasons are made known to him.

Accept the arrangement. It is not sinful. Sinfulness is personal, and can be judged only by personal knowledge of the couple. If they are leading decent, orderly, and reputable lives, no one has the right to condemn them. And, apart from personal knowledge, the arrangement has social advantages.
Advise him to follow the admired and respected people who regard an unmarried couple sharing a home as living in sin, because their view is more likely to be right than yours.

I should advise the person to make short trips on foot or on bicycle, rather than on a self-balancing motor scooter, because the latter is noisy and constantly needs repair, whereas walking and bicycling are quiet and involve little expense.
